body:
How satellites provide useful information

Artificial satellites are objects placed in orbit around the Earth to perform specific functions. Some satellites help users determine their location, while others observe the Earth's surface, atmosphere and oceans. These functions are related to space technology, but they answer different questions.

Two basic purposes

  • Satellite navigation: Helps a receiver determine where it is, supports movement towards a destination and provides accurate time.
  • Earth observation: Collects information about the Earth's surface, atmosphere or oceans without requiring a sensor to touch the area being studied.

For example, a fishing boat may use satellite-navigation signals to determine its position. Satellite observations may separately help scientists study sea-surface conditions or monitor a developing cyclone. The first application concerns the location of the boat; the second concerns environmental conditions.

How satellite navigation works

A navigation satellite broadcasts signals containing information about its position and the time of transmission. A compatible receiver measures the signals received from multiple satellites and calculates its own position. It can then express that position through geographic coordinates such as latitude and longitude.

Latitude describes how far north or south a place lies from the Equator. Longitude describes how far east or west it lies from the Prime Meridian. Together, they identify a location on the Earth.

In ordinary satellite-navigation calculations, signals from at least 4 satellites are needed to determine position and correct the receiver's clock error. The same technology can therefore provide both location information and precise time.

GNSS and GPS are not identical terms

Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) is the general term used for satellite-navigation systems. GPS is the name of the United States navigation system; it is not the name of every satellite-navigation system. India's NavIC is a regional satellite-navigation system.

How Earth observation becomes useful information

Remote sensing means obtaining information about an object or area without making physical contact with it. Earth-observation satellites carry sensors that detect energy reflected or emitted by the Earth's surface, atmosphere or oceans.

The observations are received and processed on the ground. They may then be presented as satellite images, geographical maps, measurements or thematic information. A thematic map represents a particular subject, such as vegetation, water bodies or land use. A Geographic Information System (GIS) helps organise and analyse information associated with locations.

Thus, satellite imagery can show the condition of agricultural land, while navigation coordinates can identify a particular place within that land. The two kinds of information can be used together without becoming the same thing.

India's systems and portals

India has developed different services for these purposes:

  • NavIC: India's regional satellite-navigation system.
  • GAGAN: A system that improves GPS-based navigation, particularly for civil aviation.
  • Bhuvan: A platform for viewing and using geographical information and satellite imagery.
  • Bhoonidhi: A hub for discovering and obtaining Earth-observation satellite data.
  • VEDAS: A platform for exploring and analysing information derived from Earth observations.
  • MOSDAC: A centre for meteorological and oceanographic satellite data.

The first 2 are navigation systems or services. The remaining 4 are data and information portals. A portal is a means of accessing information; it is not itself a satellite constellation.

Prelims focus

  • Navigation determines position and supports precise timing.
  • Remote sensing obtains information without physical contact with the observed area.
  • GPS is a United States system; GNSS is the general term.
  • At least 4 satellite signals are ordinarily needed for an independent navigation receiver to calculate position and correct clock error.
  • NavIC and GAGAN are navigation-related; Bhuvan, Bhoonidhi, VEDAS and MOSDAC provide access to space-derived information.
  • Trap: A satellite-navigation service and a satellite-imagery portal perform different primary functions.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 2, Globe: Latitudes and Longitudes, printed pp. 10–13; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, chapter 7, Introduction to Remote Sensing, printed pp. 84–90; ISRO, FAQ Navigation, questions 3, 9, 11 and 12; ISRO, ISRO Portals directory (official websites consulted 4 November 2026).]

body:
Meaning and purpose of NavIC

NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation. It is India's regional satellite-navigation system, developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It was earlier known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS). The name NavIC was adopted in April 2016.

NavIC was designed to give India an independently controlled system for positioning, navigation and timing, commonly abbreviated as PNT. Its independent design means that the system is intended to calculate a user's position within its service region without depending on a foreign navigation constellation such as GPS.

This independence is an important distinction between the design of NavIC and the role of GAGAN, which enhances GPS signals rather than providing an entirely separate navigation constellation.

Regional coverage

NavIC is a regional, not a global, navigation system. Its specified primary service region includes India and an area extending approximately 1,500 km beyond the Indian boundary.

A global navigation system is intended to serve users worldwide, whereas a regional system concentrates on a defined geographical area. The term regional therefore describes NavIC's intended coverage, not the nationality of people who may use it.

What information does NavIC provide?

NavIC is designed for 3 connected functions:

  • Positioning: Finding the location of a receiver.
  • Navigation: Using position information to guide movement towards a destination or along a route.
  • Timing: Providing accurate time information that can support synchronisation between systems.

These functions have applications in road transport, maritime movement, location-based services, surveying and time synchronisation. A vehicle-tracking device, for example, can use supported navigation signals to determine its location. A coastal vessel can use position information while travelling near Gujarat's coastline.

NavIC services

NavIC has 2 principal navigation-service categories:

  • Standard Positioning Service (SPS): The civilian positioning service, intended for general users with compatible receivers.
  • Restricted Service (RS): An encrypted service intended for authorised users, particularly strategic applications.

The distinction concerns who can use the service. It does not mean that the civilian service is provided by a different country's satellite system.

Basic structure of the system

NavIC has 3 basic segments. Its space segment consists of navigation satellites. Its ground segment maintains and monitors the system and prepares the information transmitted through satellites. Its user segment consists of receivers that use the transmitted signals.

The original NavIC design specified a constellation of 7 satellites: 3 geostationary and 4 inclined geosynchronous satellites. These terms describe the intended orbital arrangement. A geostationary satellite appears fixed above one region of the Equator as seen from Earth, while an inclined geosynchronous satellite follows a repeating path that is not fixed at one point in the sky.

The original constellation size is a design fact. It must not be confused with the number of satellites actually capable of providing navigation service on a particular date.

Operational status at the 4 November 2026 content cutoff

In a parliamentary reply dated 29 July 2026, the Department of Space reported that 3 NavIC satellites were available for positioning, navigation and timing services: IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01. Since at least 4 operational satellites are required for an independent position calculation, the Department stated that standalone NavIC positioning was not available at that time. It also stated that NavIC's timing service remained functional and that NavIC signals could be used with other navigation constellations.

ISRO subsequently reported that NVS-03 was launched on 30 October 2026 and that an initial orbit-raising manoeuvre was completed on 31 October 2026. Further manoeuvres were still planned. That update did not establish that NVS-03 had completed commissioning or restored standalone positioning. Therefore, the 29 July operational count should be identified by its date rather than presented as a newly verified count for 4 November 2026.

How to interpret an exam statement

The statement NavIC is designed as India's independent regional navigation system describes the system's purpose and architecture. It is correct.

The statement NavIC was independently providing standalone positioning through its original 7 operational satellites throughout 2026 would not follow from the available official evidence. The original design, the number of healthy satellites and the availability of a complete positioning service are separate matters.

Prelims focus

  • NavIC: Navigation with Indian Constellation.
  • Earlier name: Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS).
  • Name adopted in April 2016.
  • Coverage: India and approximately 1,500 km beyond its boundary.
  • Original design: 7 satellites; civilian SPS and authorised Restricted Service.
  • Trap: Independent system design must not be mistaken for confirmed standalone positioning availability on a particular date.

[References: ISRO, FAQ Navigation, questions 1, 5, 6 and 9–14; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services, section Navigation with Indian Constellation; Department of Space, Parliamentary Question: Operational Status of NavIC Constellation, Lok Sabha written reply, 29 July 2026; ISRO, Orbit Manoeuvring of NVS-03 Spacecraft, 31 October 2026 (official websites consulted 4 November 2026).]

title: NavIC: India's Regional Satellite Navigation System

body:
What is GAGAN?

GAGAN stands for GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation. It is a Satellite-Based Augmentation System (SBAS) established jointly by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India (AAI). AAI operates and maintains the system.

GAGAN was developed primarily to improve the accuracy and reliability of GPS-based navigation for civil aviation in Indian airspace. Its function is not to replace GPS with a completely independent Indian navigation constellation.

Satellite-based augmentation

An augmentation system improves an existing satellite-navigation service by supplying additional information. GAGAN supplies correction messages and integrity information relating to GPS.

Why aircraft need more than ordinary position information

Aircraft use navigation information while travelling between airports and approaching a runway. In these situations, it is important not only to obtain a position but also to know whether the navigation information is sufficiently dependable for the intended operation.

Three related ideas are useful:

  • Accuracy: How close the reported position is to the actual position.
  • Availability: Whether the required navigation service can be used when it is needed.
  • Integrity: Whether the system can provide a timely warning when navigation information should no longer be trusted for the intended operation.

GAGAN improves GPS performance through corrections and integrity messages. Integrity is particularly important in aviation because a position estimate may appear normal even when an error has become unacceptable for a safety-critical operation.

How GAGAN works at a basic level

Ground reference stations monitor GPS signals and help identify errors affecting their use. The system processes these observations to prepare correction and integrity messages. Geostationary satellites relay these messages over the service region. A compatible aircraft receiver can use them along with GPS signals.

The important relationship is that GPS supplies the underlying navigation signals, while GAGAN supplies information that improves the use and trustworthiness of those signals.

GAGAN and NavIC: the central distinction

FeatureNavICGAGAN
Primary purposeIndia's own regional positioning, navigation and timing systemImprovement of GPS-based navigation
System typeIndependent regional navigation system by designSatellite-based augmentation system
Main service informationNavigation and timing signalsGPS corrections and integrity messages
Primary emphasisRegional positioning, navigation and timingSafety-related civil aviation navigation
Principal Indian organisationsISROISRO and AAI

NavIC's independent architecture is distinct from its dated operational availability. GAGAN's dependence on GPS, by contrast, is part of its basic purpose: it is designed to augment another system.

GAGAN also differs from weather-information portals. It helps aircraft determine reliable navigation information; it is not primarily a service for viewing cloud images, rainfall maps or sea-surface temperatures.

Service status and a useful historical fact

ISRO records that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) certified GAGAN for Required Navigation Performance (RNP) 0.1 services on 30 December 2013 and for Approach with Vertical Guidance (APV-I) services on 21 April 2015. These are historical certification dates, not statements about the operational status of every airport or aircraft.

GAGAN's primary function remains the provision of satellite-based GPS augmentation for aviation. Its use by a particular aircraft depends on appropriate equipment, supported procedures and the applicable service conditions.

Prelims focus

  • GAGAN: GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation.
  • GAGAN is an SBAS, not an independent GNSS constellation.
  • It was established jointly by ISRO and AAI.
  • AAI operates and maintains GAGAN.
  • GAGAN provides GPS correction and integrity messages, primarily for civil aviation.
  • Trap: NavIC's purpose is independent regional navigation; GAGAN's purpose is augmentation of GPS.

[References: ISRO, FAQ Navigation, questions 15 and 16; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services, section GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation, including DGCA certification dates (official website consulted 4 November 2026).]
